opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you want the robot to actually do, and I'd say there's a bit of a tendency in the field to jump straight to the most complex hand possible because that's what humans have. But if you look at a lot of the useful tasks in, say, logistics or manufacturing, you can get surprisingly far with fairly simple grippers: parallel jaw grippers, maybe a suction cup. A lot of the value comes from the rest of the body: being able to walk to the right place, keep your balance, position the arm well, use whole-body motion to reach or to push things.

That said, I don't think simple grippers are the end state. If the goal is a general-purpose humanoid that can operate in environments built for people, using our tools, opening all kinds of containers, handling cables or soft objects, then at some point you need more dexterity. The question is more about timing and about where the bottleneck is. Right now, I'd argue the bottleneck isn't really the hardware of the hand. There are pretty capable dexterous hands out there. The bottleneck is the control and the data: how do you actually learn to use twenty-plus degrees of freedom robustly, with good tactile sensing, in contact-rich situations?

In simulation we've seen that reinforcement learning can produce really impressive in-hand manipulation, but transferring that to the real world is still harder than for locomotion. Contact dynamics are tricky to simulate accurately, sensing is limited, and the hands themselves are often fragile. So the hardware has to be robust enough to survive learning and deployment, which is something people underestimate.

So my view is: start with the simplest end-effector that solves the tasks you care about, get the whole-body capabilities really solid, and then add dexterity as the learning methods and the hardware mature. Eventually, yes, I think humanoids will have quite dexterous hands, but it's a progression rather than something you need on day one.

r001.rationale: The response says the field tends to favor complex hands because humans have them, but it does not identify human imitation learning as a major reason companies develop dexterous hands.

r002.rationale: It says simpler grippers can handle many useful tasks, but does not connect that to learning behaviors without imitating human actions.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and my honest answer is that I think dexterous hands are both overrated and underrated at the same time, depending on which part of the problem you're looking at.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at what humans actually do with their hands most of the day, a surprising amount of it doesn't require twenty-plus degrees of freedom. Carrying a box, opening a door, pushing a cart, picking up a cup, placing something on a shelf. A lot of that is achievable with a fairly simple gripper, maybe with a couple of extra degrees of freedom, as long as the rest of the body is doing its job. And that's the part I think people underestimate: whole-body coordination. A lot of what looks like hand dexterity in humans is really the arm, the torso, the legs, all repositioning so the hand doesn't have to be that clever. If you can walk up to the object, squat, lean in, and adjust your posture, you've already solved most of the problem before the fingers touch anything.

So from a learning perspective, I'd rather have a robust, reliable, simple end effector and a body that can move anywhere and position it well, than a very fancy hand on a body that's rigid and awkward.

Now, the other side. There is a long tail of tasks where you genuinely need fine manipulation. In-hand reorientation, handling deformable things, tools that were designed for a human hand, cables, small parts. If the goal is a general-purpose humanoid that can do what a person can do in an unstructured environment, you eventually can't avoid that. And the argument for the humanoid form factor in the first place is that the world is built for humans, which includes the hand.

The difficulty is that dexterous hands are hard on every axis at once. Mechanically they're fragile, they're expensive, tactile sensing is still immature, and from the learning side the contact dynamics are brutal. Simulation, which is where a lot of my work lives, is much less reliable for fine finger-object contact than it is for locomotion. With legged robots, we got sim-to-real to work well because the contact is relatively simple: a foot hits the ground. With a hand, you have many small, soft, intermittent contacts, and the gap between sim and real becomes much larger. So the techniques that worked so well for walking don't transfer for free.

My view on how this plays out is that it's a staged thing. First, get the humanoid to be really good at whole-body mobility and coarse manipulation with simpler hands, because that already unlocks a lot of useful work and it gives you a platform that survives in the real world. Then increase hand complexity as the sensing, the hardware, and the learning methods mature, probably with a lot more real-world data than we've needed for locomotion. I don't think you should start by trying to put the most dexterous hand possible on the robot, because you'll spend all your time fixing fingers instead of learning behaviors.

So, do we need them eventually? Yes, I think so, if we're serious about generality. Do we need them now to make humanoids useful? I'd say much less than people assume.

astra-6.text:
I think it really depends on what you want the robot to do. A human hand is incredibly versatile, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you need all of that complexity to do useful work. For a lot of tasks, a fairly simple gripper can get you quite far, and it makes the hardware and the control problem easier.

If you want a humanoid to do a very broad range of tasks in an environment designed for humans, then dexterity becomes more important. But I wouldn’t say that you need to solve the full human hand before you can have a useful humanoid. I’d start with the tasks you care about and ask how much dexterity those actually require.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it really depends on the task. We tend to look at a human hand and assume a humanoid needs all of that dexterity, but there are a lot of useful things you can do with a much simpler gripper. If you’re carrying a box or moving objects around a warehouse, you may not need five independently controlled fingers.

And there’s a tradeoff: more dexterity gives you more possibilities, but it also adds complexity in the hardware and in control. You need something that’s reliable, that can withstand contact, and that you can actually learn to use.

So I would start from the tasks you want the robot to perform and ask what capabilities those tasks require. For more general manipulation, dexterous hands become very interesting. But I don’t think you need to solve the full human hand before a humanoid can be useful.
